As Strong as Applause, As Close as Seoul and Jakarta 
 KARYA TULIS As Strong as Applause, As Close as Seoul and Jakarta
 I used to be a Korean child in Indonesia, and now I am a Korean who has to explain Indonesia to other Koreans.
 29 Okt 2026 07:30 WIB · Internasional 
 KOMPAS/ADRYAN YOGA PARAMADWYA
 Kecil Sedang Besar Sangat Besar Share
 Copy Link
 By Roh Eunbee, Warga Negara Korea Selatan, DJ dan penulis skrip bahasa Indonesia KBS World Radio. 
 This article has been translated using AI. See original . 
 00:00 00:00 10 10 1.00x I'm Korean, growing up in Indonesia. When I was a child, South Korea wasn't as well-known as it is today. K-pop wasn't widely heard, Korean dramas weren't a daily staple, and Korean artists weren't part of the conversations of young Indonesians.
 I still remember, back then, Korea started to gain popularity after the 2002 World Cup. From there, Korean dramas slowly entered Indonesia. K-pop then followed. Little by little, the Korea I once had to explain to my friends transformed into a Korea they knew, followed, and even loved. At the time, I never imagined that things would one day turn around.
 In 2008, I moved to Korea to study. This time, I found myself on the other side. When I mentioned that I grew up in Indonesia, many Koreans were not very familiar with the country. Some even thought that Bali was a separate nation.
 "For me, that experience felt strange. I used to be a Korean child in Indonesia, and now I find myself as a Korean explaining Indonesia to other Koreans. However, Indonesia is gradually changing in their eyes."
 More and more Indonesians are coming to Korea to study, work, travel, and pursue their dreams. Conversely, more and more Koreans are getting to know Indonesia, not only through Bali, but also through friends, colleagues, students, athletes, and various other firsthand experiences. We can even see this change in the world of K-pop.
 Loudi paved the way as the first Indonesian to become a Korean idol through the boy group 14U in 2017. Dita Karang followed, debuting in 2020. Carmen followed with Hearts2Hearts in 2025, and many more Indonesians have pursued careers as idols in Korea. For some, this might just be the story of a few young people who have successfully realized their dreams of becoming idols. For me, the meaning is certainly deeper.
 In the past, I was a Korean child in Indonesia who had to explain to my friends what Korea was like. Now, I see young Indonesians coming to Korea and introducing Koreans to Indonesia. It turns out that the platform for bringing the two countries together extends beyond the entertainment industry.
 I have felt the same way in recent years, particularly in the realm of sports. Megawati, for instance, has become a well-known name, not just among volleyball fans in Korea, but also among nearly all Koreans. Nicknamed "Megatron," Megawati played for two seasons with the Red Sparks. For the 2026/2027 season, she will continue her career with Hyundai E&C Hillstate.
 Her presence goes beyond just competitions and achievements on the field. Behind every athlete representing Indonesia is a country being introduced to people who may not have been familiar with it before.
 The direction of the exchange has also reversed. Shin Tae-yong, the South Korean coach, previously led the Indonesian national team and has become a well-known figure in Indonesia through football. In September 2026, FC Seoul and Persib Bandung will face off in the AFC Champions League Two.
 Matches like this bring together two nations, not in conference rooms, but in a way that resonates more closely with people's lives. Players compete, supporters cheer, and for a few hours, Seoul and Bandung feel much closer. It is here that I see the power of sports as a cultural bridge between the two countries.
 This exchange has far-reaching effects that extend beyond mere competition. When athletes and coaches move from one country to another, they bring not only their skills and experiences but also stories about their homelands. This fosters curiosity, interest, and even new connections between the people of both nations.
 An Indonesian athlete receiving support in Korea may return home with stories about the country. A Korean coach who once worked in Indonesia might take back memories of his time there. A fan who has met supporters from other nations could come home with a new friend. Sports have taught me something simple: perhaps we don’t always need to speak the same language to understand one another.
 The role of young people in strengthening the relationship between Indonesia and Korea, in my view, stems from experiences like these. It is not always about grand or official events, but rather through aspects that resonate with their daily lives, such as the music they listen to, the matches they watch, the content they share, the places they visit, the education they pursue, and the jobs they hold.
 Watching matches, following athletes' journeys, sharing their stories on social media, encouraging friends to try sports or cultures from other countries, or simply offering support to someone struggling far from home—all these are small gestures of human connection. While the support of a single individual may not alter the relationship between two nations, if thousands of young people engage in similar actions, it can gradually foster something greater: curiosity, appreciation, and a sense of closeness.
 Small matters like these may not make headlines, but it is precisely through these simple meetings that relationships can feel more human. As a Korean, I believe we do not always need to seek grand gestures to strengthen ties between Indonesia and Korea. Sometimes, it is enough to open our hearts to get to know one another, stand on the sidelines, and applaud someone who is striving.
 "I hope that the relationship between Indonesia and Korea goes beyond mere admiration from one side to the other. I want that one day, when a young Indonesian visits Korea, they do not feel like they are entering a foreign place. Similarly, when a young Korean travels to Indonesia, they should also encounter familiar faces."
 Our languages are different. The songs we listen to are different. Even the ways we celebrate victories may vary. However, perhaps that is where the beauty lies. Strengthening relationships does not mean making two countries identical; rather, it means making the differences between them easier to understand.
 And perhaps it all begins in a field. From an athlete who dares to step into a foreign land, from a supporter who arrives waving their national flag, from a young person who chooses to support rather than just watch. Then, amidst the cheers in different languages, one message will resonate universally: "We support you. You are not alone."
 If that voice continues to resonate from Seoul to Jakarta and from Jakarta back to Seoul, perhaps one day the distance between the two countries will no longer feel like thousands of kilometers apart. As long as there are people willing to bridge that gap, Seoul and Jakarta will always have a reason to feel closer together.
